DECISION1_OPTS.t: A. Trust it, since the JSON parses without error
DECISION1_OPTS.why: Parsing without error only tells you the SYNTAX was fine. It says nothing about the 8% missing an optional field or the 1% with a value outside your allowed set, both of which parse cleanly and still break the downstream API.

DECISION1_OPTS.t: B. Retry every response automatically, just in case
DECISION1_OPTS.why: Retrying everything wastes a model call and money on the 91% of responses that were already fine, and it doesn't even fix the problem: a retried call can produce the exact same missing field or bad enum value again, nothing about a retry guarantees a different outcome.

DECISION1_OPTS.t: C. Validate the schema, and explicitly handle the missing-field and invalid-value cases before the API call
DECISION1_OPTS.why: This is the only option that acts on what you actually know: two specific, named failure modes with measured rates. A schema validator that checks required-vs-optional correctly and checks enum membership catches both before they ever reach the downstream API, which is exactly the kind of check a service boundary needs.

DECISION1_OPTS.t: D. Ask the model to "be more careful" in the prompt
DECISION1_OPTS.why: A stronger instruction can lower the RATE (this module's few-shot lesson), it can't lower it to zero, and it does nothing for the two specific failure modes you've already measured. You have real data on how this model behaves; engineer around the data, don't just ask nicer.

PIPE_SAMPLES.label: Prose refusal
PIPE_SAMPLES.text: I can't set a priority without more information from the customer.

q1Options.text: Validate and parse it before trusting it, exactly as if it came from any other untrusted external source
Trust it directly, the instruction plus examples make malformed output effectively impossible
q1Options.reason: Instructions and examples reduce the RATE of malformed output, they don't reduce it to zero, a production system still needs to validate.

q1Options.text: Log a warning but proceed with whatever text came back
q1Options.reason: Logging a warning after already acting on unvalidated data doesn't prevent the corruption or crash that malformed data can cause, validation has to happen before use, not after.

q2Options.text: The system role, stated once, reinforced with an example
Anywhere in the user message, position doesn't matter
q2Options.reason: Position does matter in practice, instructions buried mid-message compete with the actual request for the model's attention, a standing instruction belongs in the system role.

q2Options.text: It should be repeated in every assistant turn instead of stated once
q2Options.reason: A standing instruction doesn't need to be repeated every turn if it's placed in the system role, that's exactly what the system role is for, persistent instructions that apply for the whole conversation.

q3Options.text: Validation, the JSON is syntactically fine, the repair pass has nothing to fix
Repair pass, this is exactly what stripping trailing commas is for
q3Options.reason: There's no syntax problem here to repair, {"name": "Sam"} parses successfully, the issue is that the resulting DATA is incomplete, which is what validation checks for, not the repair pass.

q3Options.text: Neither, this response should be accepted as-is
q3Options.reason: The response is missing a field your schema explicitly requires, accepting it as-is means your program later fails (or behaves wrong) when it tries to use the missing age field.

q4Options.text: A concrete example removes ambiguity a prose description leaves open (nesting, extra fields, exact key names)
Examples make the prompt longer, and longer prompts are always more reliable
q4Options.reason: Length itself isn't what helps, a long, vague description doesn't outperform a short, concrete example. It's the removal of ambiguity that matters, not the character count.

q4Options.text: Examples let the model skip following the system instructions entirely
q4Options.reason: Examples work alongside the system instructions, reinforcing them concretely, they don't replace or let the model ignore those instructions.
